title: Sales Enablement: Enterprise Playbook - Positioning, Pricing, Decks, Case Studies & Security FAQ
author: Avery Chen
content:
Overview:

This playbook is the canonical sales enablement reference for enterprise opportunities where customers evaluate inference platforms for production LLM workloads. It combines succinct positioning and messaging, competitive brief highlights, a recommended pitch deck outline and talking points, practical pricing guidance for Hosted/Dedicated/Private modes, two short case studies with measurable outcomes, a prospect-facing Security FAQ, common objections and rebuttals, and a sales checklist for deal progression. Use this page for SDR handoffs, AE enablement, SE prep, and customer discovery touchpoints.

Audience:
- Account Executives (AE)
- Solutions Engineers (SE)
- Sales Engineers and Sales Leaders
- Customer Success Managers during expansion

1) Executive positioning and messaging

Elevator pitch (30s):
Redwood Inference is a developer-first inference platform that delivers predictable, cost-efficient, and low-latency LLM serving across hosted, reserved (Dedicated), and private deployments - so engineering teams can ship production LLM features without owning the full inference stack.

Value pillars (talking points):
- Predictable performance & SLAs: Tail latency SLOs, dedicated capacity options, and built-in fallbacks keep user experiences consistent.
- Cost control & unit economics: Intelligent batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization playbooks reduce token cost while preserving quality.
- Unified developer experience: Same API, SDKs, and rollout tools across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.
- Enterprise-ready security & compliance: VPC/private control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and SOC2-level controls.

Target personas & discovery questions:
- Product/Eng Lead: "What latency and throughput targets do you need for peak traffic?"
- ML/Infra Lead: "Do you need model version pinning, in-house quantized variants, or predictable reserved GPU capacity?"
- Security/Compliance: "What controls do you need around data residency, key management, and auditability?"
- Finance: "What is your monthly token volume and acceptable cost per 1K tokens/embedding?"

Key differentiators (one-liners for pitch):
- Unified runtime across deployment modes - same API, observability, and rollout controls.
- Cost-aware controls (batching + cache + quantization) with measurable unit economics.
- Production-first tooling: model rollouts, per-route dashboards, and regression monitoring tied to prompt sets.

2) Competitive brief (high level)

Competitive landscape summary (use during discovery when customers mention competitors):
- Managed LLM API vendors (simple, fast onboarding, but limited deployment modes): Redwood competes on performance transparency and enterprise controls; emphasize Dedicated & Private options.
- Cloud vendor managed endpoints (broad infra, integrated cloud services): Redwood competes on inference-optimized runtime and cost controls; emphasize lower per-token costs for production workloads and richer developer ergonomics.
- Open-source/self-hosted runtimes (flexible, but heavy ops burden): Redwood competes on operational lift reduction and unified support for rollouts/observability.

Competitive win themes / messaging hooks:
- "We reduce ops by X (illustrative): typically 40-60% less engineering time to reach production compared to self-hosting a comparable stack."
- "We lower per-token costs for production chat by 10-30% through caching and batching best-practices (customer-dependent)."

Quick competitive objection responses:
- Objection: "We already use cloud vendor endpoints."
  - Rebuttal: "Many customers start on cloud endpoints and migrate to Redwood for predictable latency, cost control, and enterprise rollout features. We support staged migrations with traffic split and can serve as a drop-in routing layer while you evaluate economics."
- Objection: "We host ourselves to control costs."
  - Rebuttal: "Self-hosting often hides maintenance and reliability headwinds. For predictable throughput and lower total cost of ownership, customers choose reserved Dedicated capacity or Private deployments with our ops toolset. We also provide quantization and model recommendations to reduce GPU costs without major engineering lift."

3) Pitch deck outline & slide-level talking points

Recommended deck structure (10-12 slides):
1. Title / Hook: Customer name + one-line value (e.g., "Reduce inference cost and improve tail latency for [Product]").
2. Problem statement: Latency variability, spiraling token costs, rollout risk, and ops burden.
3. Market context: growth of LLM features and need for predictable serving.
4. Redwood solution overview: deployment modes and unified API.
5. Architecture diagram: show hosted, dedicated, and private deployment paths + routing/fallback.
6. Performance highlights: typical P95/P99 numbers on representative models and hardware (see appendix for benchmarks).
7. Cost controls: batching, cache, quantization; sample math on savings.
8. Security & compliance: VPC, KMS, audit logs, SOC2 evidence.
9. Customer case study snapshot: ROI and metrics.
10. Pricing and contract options: Hosted, Dedicated commits, Private licensing.
11. Pilot / next steps: pilot scope, success criteria, timeline.
12. Appendix: detailed benchmarks, SLOs, integration checklist.

Slide talking tips (SE notes):
- Use customer-specific numbers wherever possible (requests/sec, peak concurrency, target latency).
- Call out rollback and canary features when customers raise reliability concerns.

4) Pricing guidance & commercial models

High-level product pricing models (sales guidance):
- Hosted API (usage-based): per-token generation + per-embedding unit pricing; tiers for support and retention.
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): monthly or annual GPU pool commits, predictable throughput, and optional burst capacity.
- Private (on-prem/VPC): platform license + deployment/ops fee + optional support tiers.

Commercial structuring guidance (examples and guardrails):
- Hosted: Provide a 3-month pilot with usage discounts (e.g., 20% off first 3 months) for new enterprise accounts and SLA add-ons as upsell.
- Dedicated: Commit tiers typically start at the equivalent of ~4 A100-class GPUs sustained. Typical contract sizes for mid-market customers are $60k-250k/year depending on commit and support.
- Private: License + onboarding + annual support; average first-year ARR ranges from $250k-1.2M for large regulated customers.

Example cost comparison (simplified):
- Customer A: 500M tokens/month production traffic. Hosted baseline cost = $X/month. With caching and batching on Redwood this can reduce billed tokens by ~25-35%, resulting in annualized savings that justify Dedicated commit in 3-6 months. (Use SE to run a formal cost model with finance.)

Discounting policy & approvals:
- Discounts >25% or multi-year commitments require Revenue Operations (RevOps) approval.
- Any legal concessions on data residency or indemnity must engage Legal and Security.

5) Case studies (sales snippets you can share)

Case study: Fintech conversational support (anonymized) - Challenge: Chat product experienced 700ms median latency and high monthly inference spend during peak.
- Redwood solution: Moved to Dedicated GPU pool + prefix caching and adaptive batching; implemented model variant routing for heavy queries.
- Outcome: Median latency reduced from 700ms to 180ms; 40% reduction in monthly inference spend in 90 days; improved NPS for chat feature by 6 points.

Case study: Healthcare document summarization (anonymized) - Challenge: Regulatory requirement for data residency and audit logs; heavy embedding workload for search and indexing.
- Redwood solution: Private deployment in customer's VPC with KMS integration and fine-grained audit logging; optimized embeddings pipeline with batching and quantization.
- Outcome: Compliance posture met for regulated workloads; per-embedding cost reduced by 22%; search latency improved 2x.

Notes on sharing: Use anonymized names unless PR approved. For detailed ROI numbers share the formal case study asset with marketing.

6) Security FAQ for prospects (concise answers SEs can use verbatim)

Q: How does Redwood handle customer data in the Hosted API?
A: By default, customer requests and responses are encrypted in transit (TLS 1.2+/TLS 1.3) and at rest. Hosted customer data used for service improvement is opt-in and subject to contractual terms; enterprise customers can request no-data-retention options or choose Dedicated/Private deployments for full data isolation.

Q: Do you support private networking (VPC) and on-prem deployments?
A: Yes. We offer VPC peering for Dedicated and a Private deployment option (VPC-hosted control plane or on-prem packaging) for regulated workloads. Private deployments can be configured to avoid sending inference data to our hosted control plane.

Q: How are encryption keys managed?
A: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and support bring-your-own-key (BYOK) models. For Private deployments, we support HSM-backed key management.

Q: What compliance reports and certifications do you provide?
A: Redwood holds SOC2 Type II and maintains relevant compliance artefacts. We provide SOC2 reports under NDA and can support customer audits with evidence packages. For customers in regulated industries we run additional due-diligence and provide architecture-level controls documentation.

Q: How do you ensure model/regression quality and guard against hallucination?
A: We integrate evaluation suites and prompt-based regression monitoring into the platform. Customers can register prompt sets and automatic quality alerts; rollouts can be configured with canaries, A/B tests, and automatic fallback to verified model variants.

Q: What logging & audit capabilities are available?
A: Per-request audit logs, admin-level audit trails for configuration changes, and long-term log retention as an add-on. Logs can be forwarded to customer SIEMs via secure endpoints.

Q: Can Redwood segregate customer data and metadata?
A: Yes. Dedicated pools and Private deployments provide physical and network isolation. Metadata separation and strict RBAC controls are available in enterprise plans.

Security notes for SEs:
- Always confirm exact data flows during discovery (what PII is sent, retention expectations, SIEM integration needs).
- Escalate any unique compliance asks to Security and Legal early.

7) Common objections & rebuttals

Objection: "We need the absolute lowest latency possible."
- Rebuttal: "For ultra-low latency use cases we offer Dedicated GPU pools with tuned kernels, prefix caching, and placement policies. We can run a latency proof-of-concept using your workload to demonstrate tail latency at your target QPS."

Objection: "We cannot send data outside our VPC."
- Rebuttal: "Private deployment is designed for this: control plane can be hosted in your VPC or on-prem. We'll engage eng-private-deployments for architecture and sizing."

8) Pilot sizing and success criteria (playbook for a 6-8 week pilot)

Pilot scope checklist (numbered steps):
1. Discovery & goals: agree success metrics (e.g., P95 latency <= X ms; cost per 1K tokens <= $Y; inference uptime 99.9%).
2. Integration: API keys, network config (VPC peering if needed), and sample data ingestion.
3. Baseline run: capture current metrics for 2-4 weeks or synthetic replay if necessary.
4. Optimization run: enable caching, batching, and model variant recommendations.
5. Acceptance run: validate against success criteria for 1 week of production-like load.
6. Handoff & contract: transfer runbook, monitoring dashboards, and next-step pricing quote.

Pilot success metrics examples (use concrete numbers in proposal):
- P95 latency target: <= 300ms for interactive chat on recommended model.
- Cost target: reduce billed token units by >= 20% vs baseline.
- Reliability: 99.9% availability during pilot window.

9) Sales enablement checklist (pre-meeting and closing stages)

Pre-demo checklist:
- Confirm target API endpoints and sample prompts.
- Collect traffic profile: peak qps, avg request size (tokens), concurrency needs.
- Ask for security contact and compliance checklist.
- Prepare sample cost model (use central cost calculator).

Closing checklist (contracting & ops):
- Confirm deployment mode, commit level, and SLAs.
- Map support and escalation contacts.
- Schedule kickoff with eng-private-deployments/solutions engineering.
